profiles.meeting_scenario: An NHS hospital HIV service is preparing an internal clinical implementation plan to update its local adult antiretroviral treatment protocol and teaching materials in light of the 2008 BHIVA HIV-1 treatment guidelines. The meeting is between the consultant leading the HIV service and the clinic pharmacist who coordinates formulary-facing rollout. Their agenda is to decide what the local 'implementation pack' should contain, which patient groups need immediate review, who will draft which parts, and the timeline for circulation before the next governance meeting. The expected outcome is a shared plan for a concise local guideline package, clinician briefing, patient list review, and formulary note submission.

members.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
members.role: Consultant HIV Physician and Clinical Lead
members.expertise: HIV medicine, antiretroviral regimen selection, guideline interpretation, consultant-level service planning
members.background: Aisha leads the adult HIV clinic at a large London teaching hospital and previously contributed to regional audit work on timing of ART initiation and treatment failure management.
members.private_state: She wants a fast, clinically usable rollout that signals the service is aligned with BHIVA before the next trust governance review, while avoiding creation of a document that could be read as a rigid medico-legal standard for every edge case.
hidden_assumptions: A local implementation pack should be a short clinician-facing summary with trust-specific action points, not a comprehensive restatement of the national guideline.
The first wave of 'patients to review' means established clinic patients whose ART decisions may need changing soon, rather than newly diagnosed people not yet fully worked up.
Having the update 'ready for governance next Thursday' means a near-final draft circulated internally by close of business Wednesday so she can speak to it at the meeting.
A 'resistance section' for local planning mainly means when to send genotypes and how to use results in treatment-experienced cases, because that is where local variation causes problems.

members.name: Tom Llewellyn
members.expertise: Antiretroviral pharmacology, formulary implementation, prescribing governance, drug interaction review
members.background: Tom supports the HIV and viral hepatitis services, chairs the medicines subgroup for high-cost drugs, and routinely turns national guidance into prescribing notes and pharmacy-facing operational documents.
members.private_state: He wants the rollout to produce a document robust enough for prescribing governance and formulary scrutiny, especially around interactions, adverse events, and drug access, without generating last-minute pharmacy queries.
hidden_assumptions: A local implementation pack should include the operational prescribing detail needed by pharmacists and non-specialist prescribers, including interaction cautions, monitoring notes, and formulary wording.
The first wave of 'patients to review' includes anyone likely to be affected by initiation thresholds or co-infection guidance, including newly diagnosed patients waiting for first-line decisions.
Having the update 'ready for governance next Thursday' means the materials can still be revised up to the morning the papers are tabled, as long as a working draft exists earlier.
A 'resistance section' should cover baseline testing in treatment-naive patients as well as failure cases, because pharmacy needs the protocol to support first prescriptions.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the implementation pack
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to produce an 'implementation pack' for the BHIVA update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a concise clinician-facing package: 2-3 page summary, immediate action list, and a short teaching slide set, with reference out to the full BHIVA guideline for detail.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a fuller operational pack: prescribing summary, interaction and monitoring notes, formulary position statements, and practical pharmacy guidance alongside the clinical summary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have experience 'implementing' national guidance and the phrase naturally sounds shared; each hears their own standard deliverable in it and the meeting stays at planning level rather than enumerating every component.

misalignment_points.topic: Which patients are in the first review cohort
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with 'the patients we need to review first' after the guideline update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of existing clinic patients with low CD4 counts, virological failure, regimen toxicity, or HBV/HCV co-infection whose current management may need reconsideration.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of both existing patients and newly diagnosed adults approaching first-line initiation, because threshold and regimen guidance will affect initial prescribing choices.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely discussing the same service population in broad terms, and 'patients to review first' sounds like a pragmatic prioritization phrase rather than a category needing definition.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready for governance next Thursday' means
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on having the update 'ready for governance next Thursday'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means a polished draft circulated internally by Wednesday evening, with wording stable enough to present as the service's agreed plan.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means a usable draft can go into the governance pack and still receive substantive edits Thursday morning after pharmacy comments.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline language in hospital settings is habitually compressed and contextual; both are used to saying something is 'ready' before all edits are closed, but their thresholds for readiness differ just enough to matter later.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the resistance section
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the local package needs a 'resistance section'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means guidance on resistance interpretation and management after virological failure, especially treatment-experienced patients and when no resistance is seen despite rebound.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a protocol section covering resistance testing indications across the pathway, including baseline testing for treatment-naive patients before first prescriptions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same specialist term from the guideline table of contents, and because resistance is unquestionably relevant, neither is prompted to specify whether they mean baseline testing policy, failure management, or both.

turns.inner_thought: We need something lean and clinically usable, not a sprawling local rewrite of BHIVA. If I can get a near-final draft circulated by Wednesday evening, I can present it confidently at governance next Thursday and show we're on top of the update without boxing ourselves into a rigid standard for every edge case.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Tom. We need an implementation pack off the back of the 2008 BHIVA update before the next governance meeting, so I thought today we should just pin down what goes in it, who drafts what, and the timing to get it ready for governance next Thursday.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If we're calling it an implementation pack, it needs enough operational detail that pharmacy, the HIV team, and any non-specialist prescriber all handle prescribing consistently. I especially want the practical notes in there so we don't get a flood of last-minute interaction and access queries.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. If we're doing an implementation pack, it should help the clinic and pharmacy prescribe consistently, particularly around starting regimens, interactions, and the practical points people always ask about.

turns.inner_thought: The first job is the existing cohort already in clinic where decisions may need to change soon: low CD4, virological failure, toxicity, hepatitis co-infection. That's where the real clinical risk is and where governance will expect us to show active review.
turns.utterance: I think we should begin with the patients we need to review first. For me the urgent groups are the ones already under us with low CD4 counts, failure issues, and hepatitis co-infection, because those are the cases where the update is most likely to alter what we do in the near term.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and that same first review cohort has to include newly diagnosed adults who are about to start, otherwise we'll update the document but still have first prescriptions going out under old assumptions. Better to capture them at the outset.
turns.utterance: Agreed, and I think the patients we need to review first should also include people coming up to initial ART decisions, so we're aligned from the outset rather than catching them later.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take the consultant-facing core: when to start, what to start with, treatment failure, and the main comorbidity points. I want this implementation pack to stay concise—two or three pages plus actions and a brief slide set, with BHIVA itself doing the heavy lifting for detail.
turns.utterance: Why don't I draft the clinical summary sections on when to start, what to start with, failure, and comorbidities. I'd like the implementation pack to stay concise and focused on what people here need to change in practice.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, and I'll make sure the pack is actually usable for prescribing governance: pharmacology, adverse events, interactions, monitoring, formulary wording, the usual things pharmacy gets asked for. If I don't put that in now, we'll only end up retrofitting it under pressure.
turns.utterance: That works. I can build out the implementation pack with the pharmacology elements, adverse event reporting, interaction cautions, and the formulary wording so the teams have something operational they can use.

turns.inner_thought: We definitely need a resistance section, but mainly because clinicians will want a clear local line on genotypes and interpretation when someone rebounds or fails first line. That's where people hesitate and where local variation causes trouble.
turns.utterance: The other thing I'd definitely want included is a resistance section, because people will ask very quickly what our line is once someone has rebound or first-line failure.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, resistance needs to sit in the prescribing protocol from the beginning, including baseline testing and first-prescription checks, otherwise pharmacy gets stuck chasing whether the right work-up has happened before issuing treatment.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. I'll cover the resistance section within the prescribing protocol so it's clearly built into the checks around prescribing.

turns.inner_thought: The teaching should be brisk: key changes for registrars and nurse prescribers, not a long walk-through of every BHIVA paragraph. We need uptake, not a seminar.
turns.utterance: I also think we should do a short teaching session for the registrars and nurse prescribers, focused on the key changes rather than walking everyone through the whole national document.

turns.inner_thought: A one-page appendix would help anchor the teaching with practical prescribing steps, interactions, and monitoring. That way non-specialists have something concrete to refer to afterwards.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can attach a one-page prescribing appendix to the teaching pack so the non-specialists have the practical steps and monitoring points to hand.

turns.inner_thought: I need his sections in time to circulate a stable version by Wednesday evening. If it's still moving on Thursday morning, I can't sensibly present it as the service plan at governance.
turns.utterance: In terms of timing, I want everything ready for governance next Thursday, so could you send your material in good time for final circulation?

turns.inner_thought: That's manageable. I can get a working draft across on Wednesday, and if pharmacy throws in any final comments, I still have Thursday morning to tidy them before the papers are actually tabled. That still counts as ready.
turns.utterance: Yes, I can get you a working version by Wednesday, and if there are any final pharmacy edits needed I can polish those first thing Thursday before governance.

turns.inner_thought: Fine. I'll proceed on the basis that I'm producing the concise clinical summary and the review list for the established patients most likely to need management changes, and Tom is adding the operational pieces plus the resistance section. This should be enough to show alignment without overengineering it.
turns.utterance: Good. So I'll produce the clinical summary and the list of the patients we need to review first, and you'll prepare the operational sections of the pack and the resistance material.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll start from the BHIVA chapters on pharmacology, resistance, adverse events, and starting therapy, and turn that into something solid enough for formulary and prescribing use. As long as there's a working draft midweek, we can still refine it and have the pack ready on time.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine. I'll start from the BHIVA chapters on pharmacology, resistance, adverse events, and starting therapy, and work those into the pack so it's ready on time.
